title: Economics: Scarcity, Markets, Money, and Policy
objectives: Students will explain scarcity and identify the opportunity cost of a choice.
Students will use supply and demand tables and graphs to find the equilibrium price, shortages, and surpluses, and predict how events shift supply or demand.
Students will describe how competition affects prices and compare competitive markets with monopolies.
Students will explain the functions of money, how banks work, and the roles of the FDIC and the Federal Reserve.
Students will interpret GDP and inflation data and distinguish fiscal policy from monetary policy using neutral, evidence-based language.
teach:
Objectives

  • Explain scarcity and identify the opportunity cost of a choice (the next best alternative given up).
  • Read supply and demand tables and charts to find the equilibrium price, a shortage, or a surplus, and predict how events shift supply or demand.
  • Describe how competition affects prices and choices, and compare competitive markets with monopolies.
  • Explain the functions of money, how banks work, and the role of the Federal Reserve and the FDIC.
  • Interpret GDP and inflation data, and distinguish fiscal policy from monetary policy without taking sides in policy debates.

Materials

  • Student Lesson (printed or on screen), including the movie ticket supply and demand table
  • Study sheet (Notes) for each student
  • Whiteboard or shared screen, highlighters, calculator for percent change
  • Week 7 Social Studies practice set (12 items)

60-Minute Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5"What did you give up?" discussion and three quick questions
Direct instruction20Scarcity and opportunity cost; supply and demand; markets and competition; money and banking; GDP and inflation; fiscal and monetary policy; worked examples
Guided practice15Four economics questions worked together
Independent practice15Practice set items 1–8 (finish 9–12 at home)
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding and exit ticket from the Post Lesson

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Ask: "Think about last weekend. Name one thing you chose to do and one thing you gave up to do it." Take two or three answers and write them on the board as "Chose ___ / Gave up ___." Point out that every one of these is an economic decision: time and money are limited, so every choice costs something. Then ask:

  1. Why can't a family buy everything it wants? Answer: Its money (and time) is limited, but its wants are not. This is scarcity.
  2. When gas prices go up, what do many drivers do? Answer: Drive less, carpool, or combine trips. Higher prices lead people to buy less (the law of demand).
  3. Name one thing a bank does. Answer: Keeps people's money safe, pays interest on savings, makes loans, or processes payments (any reasonable answer).

Direct Instruction (20 minutes)

A. Scarcity and opportunity cost (3 minutes)

  • Economics is the study of how people, businesses, and governments make choices about using limited resources.
  • Scarcity means wants are unlimited but resources are limited. Because of scarcity, every choice involves a trade-off.
  • The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the next best alternative given up. Stress next best, singular: it is not the total of every option you passed up.
  • The factors of production are the resources used to make goods and services: land (natural resources), labor (human work), capital (tools, machines, buildings), and entrepreneurship (the risk-taking that combines the other three).
  • Governments face scarcity too. Money spent on one program cannot be spent on another or returned as a tax cut.

B. Supply and demand (6 minutes)

  • Demand is how much of a product buyers are willing and able to buy at each price. Law of demand: as price rises, quantity demanded falls.
  • Supply is how much sellers are willing and able to offer at each price. Law of supply: as price rises, quantity supplied rises.
  • The equilibrium price is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. In a table, find the row where the two numbers match.
  • If the price is above equilibrium, sellers offer more than buyers want: a surplus. If the price is below equilibrium, buyers want more than sellers offer: a shortage. Amount = the larger quantity minus the smaller quantity.
  • A change in price moves along the curve. Other events shift demand or supply. Demand shifters: income, tastes, the price of substitutes (goods used instead, like tea for coffee) and complements (goods used together, like printers and ink), and expectations. Supply shifters: cost of inputs, technology, weather, taxes on producers, and the number of sellers.
  • Price controls: a price ceiling is a legal maximum price (rent control is an example); if it is set below equilibrium, it causes a shortage. A price floor is a legal minimum (a minimum wage is an example); if it is set above equilibrium, it can cause a surplus. Present these neutrally: supporters point to fairness and affordability, while critics point to shortages or surpluses. GED questions ask what the data show, not which side is right.
  • Chart tip: economists usually put price on the vertical axis, but GED charts may place price on either axis. Always read the axis labels first.

C. Markets and competition (3 minutes)

  • In a market economy, prices and private choices decide what is produced. In a command economy, the government decides. The United States has a mixed economy: mostly markets, with government rules and public services. Adam Smith described the self-regulating market as an "invisible hand" in The Wealth of Nations (1776).
  • Competition among many sellers tends to push prices down and quality up, because buyers can switch.
  • A monopoly is a market with a single seller and no close substitutes. With no competitors, a monopoly can charge higher prices. An oligopoly is a market with a few large sellers (for example, airlines or wireless phone service).
  • The Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 makes it illegal for companies to agree with competitors to fix prices or to use unfair tactics to build or keep a monopoly. Note: simply being the only seller is not automatically illegal.

D. Money and banking (3 minutes)

  • Money has three functions: medium of exchange (used to buy things), unit of account (used to measure value, as in price tags), and store of value (holds value over time so it can be saved).
  • Banks accept deposits and lend part of that money to borrowers. They pay depositors interest and charge borrowers a higher interest rate; the difference is a main source of bank profit.
  • The FDIC (Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation) was created in 1933, after thousands of banks failed in the early years of the Great Depression. It insures deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each account ownership category.
  • The Federal Reserve ("the Fed") is the central bank of the United States, created by Congress in 1913. It supervises banks and conducts monetary policy. Congress has directed it to promote maximum employment and stable prices. Ordinary people do not open accounts at the Fed.

E. GDP, inflation, and policy (5 minutes)

  • GDP (gross domestic product) is the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period. It is the most common measure of the size of an economy. Real GDP is adjusted for inflation, so it shows whether the economy actually produced more.
  • When real GDP falls and unemployment rises for a sustained period, the economy is in a recession. Two quarters in a row of falling GDP is a common rule of thumb, though in the United States the official dates are set by economists at the National Bureau of Economic Research.
  • Inflation is a general rise in prices, so each dollar buys less. The Consumer Price Index (CPI), published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, is a common measure. Inflation rate = (new price − old price) ÷ old price × 100. The Fed's long-run goal is inflation of 2 percent per year.
  • Fiscal policy is the federal government's use of taxing and spending. It is set by Congress and the President through laws and the budget. The Constitution says all bills for raising revenue must start in the House of Representatives (Article I, Section 7).
  • Monetary policy is the management of interest rates and the money supply by the Federal Reserve. To cool high inflation, the Fed usually raises interest rates, which makes borrowing more expensive. To help a weak economy, it usually lowers them.
  • Stay neutral. Economists disagree about how much and when government should act. On the GED, your job is to identify each viewpoint and the evidence for it, not to choose a party.

Worked examples (model each one aloud)

Example 1: Opportunity cost. "Jordan can work an extra Saturday shift for $120, help a friend move for $60, or attend a free GED prep workshop. He chooses the workshop. Working the shift was his next best choice." What is the opportunity cost of attending the workshop?

Solution: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up. The problem says the shift was his next best choice, so the opportunity cost is the $120 shift. It is not $180 ($120 + $60), because Jordan could only have done one of those things with that Saturday. And it is not "nothing" just because the workshop was free: he still gave up the chance to earn $120.

Example 2: Reading a supply and demand table. Use the movie ticket table in the Student Lesson.

Ticket priceQuantity demandedQuantity supplied
$6300100
$8250150
$10200200
$12150250
$14100300

(a) What is the equilibrium price? (b) What happens at $14? (c) What happens at $6?

Solution: (a) Find the row where the two quantities match: at $10, 200 = 200. The equilibrium price is $10 and the equilibrium quantity is 200 tickets. (b) At $14, quantity supplied is 300 and quantity demanded is 100. Sellers offer more than buyers want: a surplus of 300 − 100 = 200 tickets. (c) At $6, quantity demanded is 300 and quantity supplied is 100. Buyers want more than sellers offer: a shortage of 300 − 100 = 200 tickets.

Example 3: Predicting a shift. "A hard freeze destroys much of the orange crop in a major growing region." What happens to the supply of oranges, the price, and the quantity sold?

Solution: Step 1: Is this about buyers or sellers? The freeze affects growers, so it is a supply event. Step 2: Direction: fewer oranges can be produced, so supply decreases. Step 3: Result: with fewer oranges available at every price, the price rises and the quantity sold falls. A common error is saying demand decreases. Buyers still want oranges; there are just fewer to sell.

Example 4: Calculating inflation. "A basket of household goods cost $80 last year and $84 this year. What was the inflation rate?"

Solution: Change: $84 − $80 = $4.
Divide by the old price: 4 ÷ 80 = 0.05.
Convert to a percent: 0.05 × 100 = 5%.
The common error is dividing by the new price (4 ÷ 84 ≈ 4.8%). Always divide by the starting value.

Example 5: Fiscal or monetary? Classify each action: (a) Congress passes a law that lowers income tax rates. (b) The Federal Reserve raises its target interest rate. (c) Congress approves new spending to repair bridges.

Solution: Ask: Who acted, and what tool did they use? (a) Congress, taxes: fiscal policy. (b) The Fed, interest rates: monetary policy. (c) Congress, spending: fiscal policy.

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

Work these together. Have students say which rule or which part of a table or chart proves each answer.

  1. In the movie ticket table, what happens if the theater charges $12? Answer: Quantity supplied is 250 and quantity demanded is 150, so there is a surplus of 250 − 150 = 100 tickets.
  2. The price of tea rises sharply. What happens to the demand for coffee? Answer: Demand for coffee increases, because tea and coffee are substitutes; some tea drinkers switch to coffee.
  3. A country's real GDP goes from $500 billion to $520 billion. By what percent did it grow? Answer: (520 − 500) ÷ 500 = 20 ÷ 500 = 0.04, so 4%.
  4. A worker's pay rises 2% in a year when prices rise 5%. Can the worker buy more or less than before? Answer: Less. Prices rose faster than pay, so the worker's purchasing power fell.

Checks for Understanding

  • "What is the difference between a shortage and a surplus?" Expected: A shortage is when quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied (price below equilibrium); a surplus is when quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded (price above equilibrium).
  • "Who controls fiscal policy, and who controls monetary policy?" Expected: Congress and the President control fiscal policy; the Federal Reserve controls monetary policy.
  • "Why is real GDP more useful than GDP that is not adjusted for prices?" Expected: Real GDP removes the effect of inflation, so it shows whether the economy actually produced more, not just whether prices went up.
  • "Name the three functions of money." Expected: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value.

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

Adding up every option for opportunity cost. Correction: opportunity cost is only the next best alternative. Ask, "If you had not made this choice, what would you have done instead?"

Mixing up shortage and surplus. Correction: "Short" means buyers are left without enough. If demanded > supplied, it is a shortage. If supplied > demanded, it is a surplus, and stores have extra on the shelves.

Confusing a price change with a shift. Correction: a product's own price change moves along the curve (quantity demanded changes). A change in income, tastes, related goods, costs, or technology shifts the whole curve.

Mixing up fiscal and monetary policy. Correction: link the words. Fiscal = taxes and spending = Congress and the President. Monetary = money and interest rates = the Federal Reserve.

Using the new value as the base in percent change. Correction: percent change always divides by the old (starting) value.

Answering policy questions with personal opinion. Correction: GED items ask what a passage or chart shows, or how two viewpoints differ. Point students back to the evidence.

Differentiation

Support: Give students a two-column organizer, "Buyers (demand)" and "Sellers (supply)," and have them sort events before predicting price changes. For tables, have them circle the matching row first, then shade rows above (surplus) and below (shortage). Provide the percent change formula on a card.

Stretch: Ask students to predict what happens when demand and supply both change (for example, a new study praises a product while a new factory opens: quantity rises, but the price change is uncertain). Have them explain why a price ceiling below equilibrium can lead to long waiting lists, and then state one argument supporters make and one argument critics make, using neutral language.

How This Shows Up on the GED

  • Economics is about 15 percent of the GED Social Studies test. Most economics questions give you a table, chart, or short reading first.
  • Typical formats: multiple choice ("Based on the table, at what price…"), drop-down sentences ("The policy described is an example of ___ policy"), drag-and-drop sorting (events that shift supply vs. demand), and fill-in-the-blank calculations (a shortage amount or a percent change).
  • Typical wording: "Which conclusion is supported by the data?", "What would most likely happen if…?", "Which statement describes the difference between the two viewpoints?", "Which sentence expresses an opinion?"
  • Remind students that answers must come from the stimulus. A choice can be true in the real world and still be wrong if the data do not support it.
student:
Why This Matters

Economics is about 15 percent of the GED Social Studies test, and it is also the subject you use every day: paying bills, comparing prices, deciding whether to take an extra shift, or wondering why groceries cost more this year. This week you will learn the core ideas and practice reading the tables and charts that GED economics questions are built on.

1. Scarcity and Opportunity Cost

Scarcity means that people's wants are unlimited, but the resources to meet them (money, time, materials, workers) are limited. Because of scarcity, every choice has a trade-off: choosing one thing means giving up something else.

Opportunity cost = the value of the next best alternative you give up when you make a choice. It is only the next best option, not every option you passed up.

Worked example 1. Keisha has a free evening. She could work overtime for $90, watch a movie with friends, or study for the GED. She studies. She says she would have worked overtime if she had not studied. What is her opportunity cost?

Step 1: What did she choose? Studying. Step 2: What was her next best choice? Overtime. Answer: The opportunity cost is the $90 she could have earned. The movie is not part of it; she could not have done all three.

Businesses use resources called the factors of production: land (natural resources), labor (workers), capital (tools, machines, buildings), and entrepreneurship (the person who takes the risk of starting the business).

2. Supply and Demand

Demand is how much buyers want to buy at each price. Law of demand: when the price goes up, people buy less. Supply is how much sellers want to sell at each price. Law of supply: when the price goes up, sellers offer more, because selling is more profitable.

The equilibrium price is the price where the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer. Markets tend to move toward this price.

Ticket priceQuantity demandedQuantity supplied
$6300100
$8250150
$10200200
$12150250
$14100300

Movie tickets per week at a small theater (hypothetical data)

Reading the table:
Demanded = supplied → equilibrium
Demanded > supplied (price too low) → shortage
Supplied > demanded (price too high) → surplus
Size of a shortage or surplus = larger number − smaller number

Worked example 2. Use the table. What is the equilibrium price, and what happens if the theater charges $14?

Step 1: Find the matching row: at $10, 200 demanded and 200 supplied. Equilibrium price = $10.
Step 2: At $14, 300 are supplied but only 100 are demanded. Supplied is bigger, so there is a surplus.
Step 3: 300 − 100 = 200 extra tickets.

On a graph, the demand line slopes one way and the supply line slopes the other way. The point where they cross is the equilibrium. Economists usually put price on the vertical axis, but a GED chart might put it on either axis, so always read the axis labels first.

What shifts supply and demand?

A change in a product's own price does not shift demand; it just changes how much people buy. Other events shift the whole curve:

  • Demand shifters (buyers): changes in income, tastes and trends, the price of a substitute (something used instead, like tea instead of coffee), the price of a complement (something used together, like a game console and games), and expectations about the future.
  • Supply shifters (sellers): the cost of materials or labor, new technology, weather and natural disasters, taxes on producers, and the number of sellers.

Worked example 3. A drought ruins much of the wheat harvest. What happens to the price of wheat?

Step 1: Who is affected, buyers or sellers? Farmers, the sellers. This is a supply change.
Step 2: Less wheat can be grown, so supply decreases.
Step 3: When supply decreases, the price rises and less wheat is sold.

Sometimes the government sets a price ceiling (a legal maximum price, such as rent control) or a price floor (a legal minimum price, such as a minimum wage). A ceiling set below equilibrium tends to cause a shortage; a floor set above equilibrium tends to cause a surplus. People disagree about whether these policies help more than they hurt. GED questions ask what the data show, not which side you are on.

3. Markets and Competition

The United States has a mixed economy. Most decisions are made by buyers and sellers in markets, but the government makes rules and provides some services. Competition among sellers usually leads to lower prices and better quality, because customers can switch. A monopoly is a market with only one seller and no close substitutes; without competitors, it can charge more. Federal antitrust laws, beginning with the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890, make it illegal for companies to fix prices with their competitors or to use unfair tactics to create or keep a monopoly.

4. Money and Banking

Money does three jobs. It is a medium of exchange (you use it to buy things), a unit of account (prices are measured in it), and a store of value (you can save it for later).

Banks take in deposits and lend part of that money out. They pay savers interest and charge borrowers a higher rate; the difference helps banks earn a profit. The FDIC, created in 1933, insures deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each type of account ownership. The Federal Reserve, created by Congress in 1913, is the nation's central bank. It is a bank for banks and for the federal government, not for individuals.

5. GDP and Inflation

GDP (gross domestic product) is the total value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year (or other period). It measures the size of an economy. Real GDP is adjusted for inflation, so it shows whether the country truly produced more. When real GDP falls and many people lose jobs, the economy is in a recession.

Inflation is a general rise in prices. When prices rise faster than your pay, your money buys less; your purchasing power falls.

Percent change (growth or inflation rate):
(new value − old value) ÷ old value × 100

Worked example 4. A price index rose from 250 to 260. What was the inflation rate?

260 − 250 = 10
10 ÷ 250 = 0.04
0.04 × 100 = 4%

6. Fiscal and Monetary Policy

Fiscal policyMonetary policy
Who decidesCongress and the PresidentThe Federal Reserve
ToolsTaxes and government spendingInterest rates and the money supply
To boost a weak economyCut taxes or increase spendingLower interest rates
To cool high inflationRaise taxes or cut spendingRaise interest rates

Economists and political leaders often disagree about which tools to use and when. Some stress the benefits of acting quickly to protect jobs; others stress the long-term costs, such as a larger national debt. On the GED, focus on what each side says and what evidence it uses.

Try It

1. Luis can spend Sunday working at a car wash for $70, babysitting for $50, or resting at home. He chooses to babysit. His next best choice was the car wash. What is the opportunity cost of babysitting?

Show answer

The $70 from the car wash, his next best alternative. Resting at home is not included.

2. In the movie ticket table, what happens if the price is $8?

Show answer

Quantity demanded is 250 and quantity supplied is 150. Demanded is bigger, so there is a shortage of 250 − 150 = 100 tickets.

3. The price of tea rises sharply. What happens to the demand for coffee?

Show answer

Demand for coffee increases. Tea and coffee are substitutes, so some tea drinkers switch to coffee.

4. A country's real GDP grew from $800 billion to $840 billion. What was the growth rate?

Show answer

840 − 800 = 40; 40 ÷ 800 = 0.05; 0.05 × 100 = 5%.

5. The Federal Reserve lowers interest rates. Is this fiscal or monetary policy, and what is it usually meant to do?

Show answer

Monetary policy. Lower rates make borrowing cheaper, which is usually meant to encourage spending and help a weak economy.
post:
Summary of Key Points

  • Scarcity forces choices. The opportunity cost of a choice is the next best alternative you give up.
  • As price rises, quantity demanded falls and quantity supplied rises. The equilibrium price is where they are equal. Below it there is a shortage; above it there is a surplus.
  • Events that affect buyers shift demand; events that affect sellers shift supply. A decrease in supply raises the price.
  • Competition tends to lower prices; a monopoly has no competitors. Antitrust laws began with the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890.
  • Money is a medium of exchange, a unit of account, and a store of value. The FDIC (1933) insures bank deposits; the Federal Reserve (1913) is the central bank.
  • GDP measures the value of final goods and services produced; real GDP adjusts for inflation. Inflation is a general rise in prices.
  • Fiscal policy (taxes and spending) belongs to Congress and the President; monetary policy (interest rates and the money supply) belongs to the Federal Reserve.

Exit Ticket

1. Define opportunity cost in one sentence.

Show answer

Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative you give up when you make a choice.

2. At a price of $5, buyers want 40 items and sellers offer 70. Is this a shortage or a surplus, and how large is it?

Show answer

A surplus, because more is supplied than demanded: 70 − 40 = 30 items.

3. New machines cut the cost of making bicycles. What happens to the supply and the price of bicycles?

Show answer

Supply increases, so the price tends to fall.

4. Congress votes to cut income taxes. Is this fiscal or monetary policy?

Show answer

Fiscal policy, because Congress changed taxes.

5. A basket of goods cost $200 last year and $210 this year. What was the inflation rate?

Show answer

(210 − 200) ÷ 200 = 10 ÷ 200 = 0.05, so 5%.

Reflection

  • Describe a recent choice you made with your time or money. What was the opportunity cost?
  • Think of a product whose price changed noticeably in the last year. Was the change more likely caused by a shift in supply, a shift in demand, or both? Explain.
  • Which skill was hardest for you this week: reading supply and demand tables, calculating percent change, or telling fiscal and monetary policy apart? What will you do to practice it?

Test-Taking Strategy: Label the Chart Before You Read It

Before you look at the answer choices on a chart or table question, spend ten seconds on the labels: the title, what each axis or column measures, and the units (dollars, billions, percent, per day). Many wrong answers come from reading the right number in the wrong column, or from mixing up "quantity demanded" and "quantity supplied." Once the labels are clear, find the exact numbers the question needs and do the math on scratch paper.

vocab.def: The basic problem that people's wants are unlimited but the resources to satisfy them are limited.
vocab.example: A family with $500 for the month cannot buy everything on its wish list.

vocab.def: The value of the next best alternative given up when making a choice.
vocab.example: If you skip a $60 shift to attend a class, the opportunity cost of the class is the $60.

vocab.def: The resources used to produce goods and services: land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship.
vocab.example: A bakery uses flour (land), bakers (labor), ovens (capital), and an owner's risk (entrepreneurship).

vocab.def: The amount of a product buyers are willing and able to buy at each price.
vocab.example: When a store cuts the price of jeans, it sells more pairs.

vocab.def: The amount of a product sellers are willing and able to offer at each price.
vocab.example: When strawberry prices rise, farmers bring more strawberries to market.

vocab.def: The price at which the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied.
vocab.example: If buyers want 200 tickets at $10 and the theater offers 200, $10 is the equilibrium price.

vocab.def: A situation in which quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied, usually because the price is below equilibrium.
vocab.example: A popular toy sells out in hours, and many shoppers leave empty-handed.

vocab.def: A situation in which quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded, usually because the price is above equilibrium.
vocab.example: Unsold winter coats pile up, so the store puts them on sale.

vocab.def: A market with only one seller of a product that has no close substitutes.
vocab.example: A town with only one water company has a monopoly on water service.

vocab.def: The price paid for borrowing money, or the amount earned for saving it, usually stated as a yearly percentage.
vocab.example: A savings account that pays 2% interest earns $2 a year on $100.

vocab.def: The total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period.
vocab.example: Economists compare GDP from year to year to see whether the economy is growing.

vocab.def: A general rise in the prices of goods and services, which reduces what each dollar can buy.
vocab.example: Groceries that cost $100 last year cost $104 this year.

vocab.def: The federal government's use of taxes and spending to influence the economy, decided by Congress and the President.
vocab.example: Congress passes a temporary tax cut during a slowdown.

vocab.def: Actions by the central bank to influence interest rates and the money supply.
vocab.example: The Federal Reserve raises interest rates to slow inflation.

vocab.def: The central bank of the United States, created by Congress in 1913, which supervises banks and conducts monetary policy.
vocab.example: News reports say the Federal Reserve held interest rates steady this month.

Week 7 Study Sheet: Economics

Scarcity: unlimited wants, limited resources. Opportunity cost: the next best alternative given up (not the total of all options).

Supply and Demand

  • Law of demand: price up → quantity demanded down
  • Law of supply: price up → quantity supplied up
  • Equilibrium: demanded = supplied
  • Shortage: demanded > supplied (price too low)
  • Surplus: supplied > demanded (price too high)
  • Size: larger quantity − smaller quantity
  • Price ceiling (legal max) below equilibrium → shortage
  • Price floor (legal min) above equilibrium → surplus

What Shifts the Curves

  • Demand: income, tastes, price of substitutes and complements, expectations
  • Supply: input costs, technology, weather, taxes on producers, number of sellers
  • Supply down → price up; supply up → price down
  • Demand up → price up; demand down → price down
Fiscal policyMonetary policy
WhoCongress and the PresidentFederal Reserve
ToolsTaxes, spendingInterest rates, money supply
Boost economyCut taxes / spend moreLower rates
Fight inflationRaise taxes / spend lessRaise rates

Money and Banking

  • Money: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value
  • Banks profit by charging borrowers more interest than they pay savers
  • FDIC (1933): insures deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category
  • Federal Reserve (1913): central bank; goals of maximum employment and stable prices
  • Sherman Antitrust Act (1890): bans price fixing and unfair monopoly tactics

Measuring the Economy

  • GDP: value of all final goods and services produced in a country
  • Real GDP: adjusted for inflation
  • Recession: economy shrinks, unemployment rises
  • Inflation: general rise in prices; purchasing power falls
  • Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100

stimuli.title: When a Second Provider Came to Town
stimuli.html:
For more than ten years, Northline Cable was the only company that offered home internet service in the small town of Harlow. Its basic plan cost $85 a month for a speed of 100 megabits per second (Mbps). Residents who were unhappy with the price or the service had nowhere else to go.

In 2023, a second company, Valley Fiber, finished laying new lines and began selling service in Harlow. Valley Fiber offered 300 Mbps for $55 a month. Within a year, Northline lowered the price of its basic plan to $60 a month and raised its speed to 300 Mbps. Northline also dropped a $10 monthly equipment fee that it had charged for years.

Economists call a market with only one seller and no close substitutes a monopoly. Being the only seller is not illegal by itself. However, federal antitrust laws, beginning with the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890, make it illegal for companies to agree with competitors to fix prices or to use unfair tactics to create or keep a monopoly.

stimuli.title: How Banks and the Federal Reserve Work
stimuli.html:
A bank is a business. It accepts deposits from customers and pays them interest, and it lends money to other customers who pay interest on their loans. A bank might pay 1 percent interest on a savings account and charge 7 percent on a car loan. The difference between the interest a bank earns on loans and the interest it pays on deposits is a major source of its profit. Banks keep only part of their deposits on hand; much of the rest is lent out.

Because banks lend out deposits, a bank can fail if many loans go unpaid or if too many depositors try to withdraw their money at once. Thousands of banks failed in the early years of the Great Depression, and many families lost their savings. In response, Congress created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) in 1933. Today, the FDIC insures deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each account ownership category. If an insured bank fails, depositors get their insured money back.

The Federal Reserve, created by Congress in 1913, is the central bank of the United States. Individuals do not open accounts there; it serves banks and the federal government. The Federal Reserve supervises banks and conducts monetary policy, mainly by influencing short-term interest rates. Congress has directed it to promote maximum employment and stable prices.

stimuli.title: Two Views on Government Action in a Recession
stimuli.html:
Economist A: When a recession hits, families and businesses cut back on spending. That drop in demand leads businesses to lay off workers, who then spend even less. During a recession, the federal government should step in by increasing spending on projects such as road and bridge repair or by cutting taxes for a limited time. Putting money into the economy can help businesses keep workers until conditions improve.

Economist B: When the federal government spends more than it collects in taxes, it must borrow the difference, and that borrowing adds to the national debt. Future taxpayers will have to pay interest on that debt. Large spending increases can also be slow to take effect. Instead, the Federal Reserve can lower interest rates, which encourages people and businesses to borrow and spend without adding to the national debt.

items.prompt: Andre has $40 left after paying his bills this week. He could buy new work boots, buy a ticket to a basketball game, or put the money in savings. He buys the boots. He says that if he had not bought the boots, he would have gone to the game. What is the opportunity cost of buying the boots?
options: The basketball game ticket
The new work boots
The basketball game ticket plus the money he could have saved
The $40 put into savings
items.hint: Opportunity cost is the next best choice, the one he would have picked instead.
items.explain:
Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up. Andre says that without the boots he would have gone to the game, so the game ticket is his next best choice and his opportunity cost.

The boots are what he chose, not what he gave up. Adding the game and savings together is wrong because he could only use the $40 once. Savings was his third choice, not his next best.

items.prompt: Based on the table, at what price does the quantity of kayak rentals demanded equal the quantity supplied?
items.hint: Look for the row where the two quantity columns show the same number.
items.explain:
At $20, quantity demanded is 60 and quantity supplied is 60. Because they are equal, $20 is the equilibrium price. On the graph, this is where the two lines cross.

At $15, 75 are demanded but only 45 supplied (a shortage). At $25, 75 are supplied but only 45 demanded (a surplus). At $30, the surplus is even larger.

items.prompt: If kayak rentals were priced at $30, how many more rentals per day would businesses offer than customers want?
items.hint: Find the $30 row. Subtract quantity demanded from quantity supplied.
items.explain:
At $30:
Quantity supplied = 90
Quantity demanded = 30
Surplus = 90 − 30 = 60 rentals per day.

A common error is reading the $35 row (105 − 15 = 90) or the $10 row, where the numbers are reversed and there is a shortage of 60, not a surplus.

items.prompt: Each event below affects the market for coffee. Drag each event into the box that shows how it changes the market for coffee.
choices: A widely reported health study finds that drinking coffee improves memory.
A frost destroys a large share of the coffee crop in a major growing region.
The price of tea, a substitute for coffee, falls sharply.
A new machine lets coffee farms harvest beans faster and at lower cost.
The government places a new tax on coffee producers for every pound they sell.
items.hint: First ask whether the event affects buyers (demand) or sellers (supply). Then decide the direction.
items.explain:
• Health study: changes buyers' tastes; more people want coffee. Demand increases.
  • Frost: farmers can produce less. Supply decreases.
  • Cheaper tea: tea is a substitute, so some coffee drinkers switch to tea. Demand for coffee decreases.
  • New machine: better technology lowers costs, so sellers can offer more. Supply increases.
  • Tax on producers: raises sellers' costs. Supply decreases.

A common error is putting the frost under "demand decreases." Buyers still want coffee; there is simply less to sell.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
options: Competition from a new company led Northline to offer customers a better deal.
Northline broke the Sherman Antitrust Act by being Harlow's only internet provider.
Valley Fiber will soon become the only internet provider in Harlow.
Internet prices in every town fell in 2023, whether or not a new company arrived.
items.hint: What did Northline change, and what happened just before it changed?
items.explain:
After Valley Fiber entered the market with a cheaper, faster plan, Northline cut its price from $85 to $60, tripled its speed from 100 to 300 Mbps, and dropped a $10 fee. This supports the conclusion that competition led Northline to offer a better deal.

The passage says that being the only seller "is not illegal by itself," so it does not support the claim that Northline broke the law. Nothing in the passage predicts Valley Fiber's future or describes prices in other towns.

items.prompt: Which statements are supported by the passage? Select two answers.
options: Banks earn money partly by charging borrowers a higher interest rate than they pay depositors.
If an FDIC-insured bank fails, its depositors get their insured money back, up to a set limit.
Individuals can open savings accounts directly at the Federal Reserve.
Banks keep all of their customers' deposits in their vaults at all times.
Congress created the Federal Reserve in response to bank failures during the Great Depression.
items.hint: Check each statement against the passage. Watch the dates: which agency was created in 1913 and which in 1933?
items.explain:
Correct: The passage says the difference between the interest a bank earns on loans and the interest it pays on deposits "is a major source of its profit," and that the FDIC insures deposits up to $250,000 so that depositors "get their insured money back."

Incorrect: The passage says individuals "do not open accounts" at the Federal Reserve, and that banks "keep only part of their deposits on hand." The Federal Reserve was created in 1913, before the Great Depression; the agency created in response to Depression-era bank failures was the FDIC (1933).

items.prompt:
Complete the statements.

Decisions about federal taxes and government spending are called {{0}}. These decisions are made by {{1}}. Decisions about interest rates and the money supply are called {{2}}. When inflation is too high, the Federal Reserve usually {{3}} interest rates to slow borrowing and spending.

options: fiscal policy
monetary policy
foreign policy
trade policy
Congress and the President
the Federal Reserve
the Supreme Court
the FDIC
monetary policy
fiscal policy
antitrust policy
tariff policy
raises
lowers
freezes

items.hint: Fiscal = taxes and spending. Monetary = money and interest rates. Higher rates make borrowing more expensive.
items.explain:
Fiscal policy is the use of taxes and spending. It is set by Congress and the President through laws and the federal budget. Monetary policy is the management of interest rates and the money supply by the Federal Reserve. To fight high inflation, the Fed usually raises interest rates; higher rates make loans more expensive, so people and businesses borrow and spend less, which eases the pressure on prices.

A common error is choosing "the Federal Reserve" for the second blank. The Fed controls monetary policy, not taxes or spending.

items.prompt: According to the graph, between which two years did Country Z's real GDP decrease?
options: Year 1 to Year 2
Year 2 to Year 3
Year 3 to Year 4
Year 4 to Year 5
items.hint: Compare each bar with the one right after it. Which bar is shorter than the bar before it?
items.explain:
Real GDP values: Year 1, 640; Year 2, 662; Year 3, 681; Year 4, 655; Year 5, 668; Year 6, 700 (billions of dollars).

From Year 3 to Year 4, real GDP fell from 681 to 655, a drop of 681 − 655 = 26 billion dollars. Every other pair of years shows an increase. Because real GDP is adjusted for inflation, this drop means the country actually produced less, which is a sign of a recession.

Year 4 to Year 5 is a common wrong choice: Year 4 is the low point, but GDP rose from 655 to 668 after it.

items.prompt: Dana's hourly wage rose from $20.00 in Year 2 to $20.60 in Year 3. Based on the table, which statement best describes what happened to Dana's purchasing power from Year 2 to Year 3?
options: It fell, because her wage rose 3% while the cost of the basket rose 5%.
It fell, because her wage rose 3% while the cost of the basket rose 4%.
It rose, because her wage went up by $0.60 an hour.
It stayed the same, because both her wage and prices went up.
items.hint: Find the percent change in her wage and the percent change in the basket's total cost from Year 2 to Year 3, then compare.
items.explain:
Wage change: $20.60 − $20.00 = $0.60; 0.60 ÷ 20.00 = 0.03 = 3%.

Price change (Year 2 to Year 3): $546 − $520 = $26; 26 ÷ 520 = 0.05 = 5%.

Prices rose faster than her pay (5% > 3%), so each hour of work buys less than before. Her purchasing power fell.

The 4% choice uses the wrong years: from Year 1 to Year 2, the basket rose from $500 to $520, and 20 ÷ 500 = 4%. A raise in dollars does not mean higher purchasing power if prices rise faster.

items.prompt: Read the news brief below about the fictional city of Riverton. Click the sentence that expresses an opinion rather than a fact that could be checked.
spans: On Tuesday, the Riverton City Council voted 5 to 2 to raise the standard bus fare from $1.50 to $2.00 beginning March 1.
According to the transit agency's annual report, the cost of running the bus system rose 18 percent over the past three years.
Fares currently cover about one-fourth of the system's operating costs, and the rest comes from city and federal funds.
Council Member Ruth Okafor, who voted no, pointed out that ridership dropped after the last fare increase.
Any city that raises bus fares during hard times has clearly forgotten the riders who depend on buses the most.
The transit agency will hold two public hearings in February to explain the change.
items.hint: A fact can be proved true or false with records or data. An opinion is a judgment that people could reasonably disagree with.
items.explain:
The sentence "Any city that raises bus fares during hard times has clearly forgotten the riders who depend on buses the most" is a judgment. Words such as "clearly forgotten" signal the writer's belief, and no record could prove it true or false.

The other sentences can be checked: the council vote and new fare are public record, the cost increase and funding shares come from the agency's report, the hearings are scheduled events, and what Council Member Okafor said is a fact about her statement (and ridership numbers can be checked).

items.skill: Predicting effects of a price ceiling
items.prompt: Suppose the Pine Lake town council sets a maximum price of $15 per kayak rental. Based on the table, what would most likely result?
options: A shortage of 30 rentals per day
A surplus of 30 rentals per day
A shortage of 60 rentals per day
75 rentals per day, enough for every customer who wants one
items.hint: Find the $15 row. Compare how many rentals customers want with how many businesses offer.
items.explain:
A legal maximum price is a price ceiling. Here it is below the equilibrium price of $20, so the price will settle at $15.

At $15:
Quantity demanded = 75
Quantity supplied = 45
Demanded is greater, so there is a shortage: 75 − 45 = 30 rentals per day.

A shortage of 60 comes from reading the $10 row. The 75-rental choice is wrong because businesses would offer only 45 rentals at $15, so 30 customers a day would go without.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the main difference between the two economists?
options: Economist A favors using fiscal policy to fight a recession, while Economist B worries about its long-term cost and prefers monetary policy.
Economist A wants the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, while Economist B wants Congress to cut taxes.
Economist A believes recessions are caused by the national debt, while Economist B believes they are caused by low interest rates.
Economist A argues that government should take no action in a recession, while Economist B argues that Congress should spend more.
items.hint: Identify which tool each economist recommends: taxes and spending, or interest rates.
items.explain:
Economist A recommends higher government spending or temporary tax cuts: these are fiscal policy tools. Economist B warns that borrowing adds to the national debt and that spending can be slow, and recommends that the Federal Reserve lower interest rates: a monetary policy tool. So A favors fiscal policy, and B is concerned about its costs and prefers monetary policy.

The other choices reverse or invent positions. Neither economist wants higher interest rates, neither explains what causes recessions, and it is B, not A, who is cautious about new spending. The question asks you to describe the viewpoints, not decide which one is right.
